newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels conference hopes 45 states will ban mines.
newsitem.headline: Brussels conference hopes 45 states will ban mines.

text.p: An international conference on landmines hopes that 45 states will commit themselves to a complete ban on anti-personnel landmines next week, the organisers said on Monday.

The Brussels Conference on a Global Ban on Antipersonnel Mines, which will run from June 24-27, builds on talks started in Ottawa, Canada last year and aims at getting as many states as possible to sign an anti-mine treaty by the end of this year.
"We hope that about 45 countries will show their commitment here," Secretary-General of the conference Andre Mernier told a news conference.
Mernier, a Belgian diplomat, said that by taking part in the conference, countries will have to come off the fence about their support for a ban on mines.
About 100 countries are expected to send representatives to the Brussels conference, which aims to agree a total ban on production, transfer, use and stockpiling of mines.

"Through the Brussels Declaration, the Conference will identify those states willing to make a political commitment... with the objective of concluding negotiations and signing a treaty by the end of 1997," the organisers said in a statement.
After a technical meeting in Oslo, Norway in September, states subscribing to the Brussels Declaration will sign an anti-mine treaty in Ottawa at the end of this year.
Although mines kill about 25,000 people per year (or one every 20 minutes) and handicap many more, diplomatic efforts to get states to sign an anti-mine treaty have had little succes.
Worldwide, some 100 million mines are waiting for a victim, mainly in war-torn third world countries, and every year more mines are placed than are removed, Mernier said.

Seperately from the "Ottawa Proces", a United Nations- sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva is also seeking a ban on mines. Talks there will run until June 27 and are set to continue at a seven-week round starting late July.
Mernier said that countries who are serious about a ban on mines did want to rely on the Geneva conference alone.
"I do not think we will get (a treaty) via the Geneva Conference. It is a consensus body which must have agreement from all members...it is a non-starter," he said.
He said that an anti-mines treaty was urgently needed, as a beacon for those countries who were not willing to sign yet.
"I know China will not sign up next year, but at least there will a norm," he said, adding that the nuclear non-proliferation treaty had had a similar pioneer function.
China and Russia, major producers and users of landmines, are not supporting the Ottawa-Brussels conference.
The United States said earlier this year it will unilaterally observe a permanent ban on the export of anti- personnel mines and seek a global ban via the Geneva conference.
"The U.S. will come to the Brussels conference, but only as an observer," Mernier said.

He added that the Brussels conference hoped to get support from the three leading European Union states. "Germany has always been on board, I have no doubt that they will sign. I think that following the change of government in France and the U.K., these countries will come aboard as well," he said.
The only treaty regulating the use of anti-personnel mines at the moment is the 1980 U.N. Conventional Weapons Convention.

At a May 1996 review of that convention in Geneva, 55 nations agreed to outlaw undetectable anti-personnel mines and restricted the use of other "smarter" types of mines, but failed to agree on a full-scale ban. Few countries have ratified the 1996 review.
